references.text: In Jesus' parable of the two debtors, he asks, "Which of them will love him most?" — both debtors owe their master, just as the debtors in the parable of the steward. [ref:Luke 7:41-42]

In the parable of the unforgiving servant, a servant is called to settle accounts with his master regarding his debt, paralleling how the steward calls each of his master's debtors to him. [ref:Matthew 18:24]
The servant asks his fellow servant, "Pay what you owe me!" — the question of what one owes (ὀφείλεις) is also central in Luke 16:5. [ref:Matthew 18:28]
Context for the verse: The steward has been accused of squandering his master's property, and it is this situation that drives him to call the debtors to secure his own future. [ref:Luke 16:1-2]
The Lord commends the dishonest steward for his shrewdness — the outcome of the action that begins in verse 5, where he calls the debtors and negotiates a reduction of their debts. [ref:Luke 16:8-9]
Paul uses the same Greek word ὀφείλω regarding debt: "Owe no one anything" — the theme of debt and debtors is central in both texts. [ref:Romans 13:8]
